text.p: By Sergio Cofferati, National Secretary of the the Confederazione Generale Italiana del Lavoro (CGIL), Italy's largest trades union confederation. (Translation by Reuters).
Italy's trade union confederations have been calling for an overall reform of the country's pension system since the second half of the 1970s.
At that time the first signs were emerging of the crisis which was to envelop all the major industrialised nations from the 1980s onwards.

The reasons are well known -- a falling birth rate, increased life expectancy, a drastic down-sizing of the industrial sector but above all a weakening in the link between economic development and jobs growth.

In Italy, in particular, a rise of more then 30 percent in the dependency ratio between the mid-1970s and the mid-1990s has been accompanied by a negative trend in contributions flowing into the system. This reflected the abnormal growth in the number of self-employed who, while still enjoying the same pension rights, are subject to contributions at rates of less than half those applied to salaried workers.

The reform called for by the major union confederations had as its first goal that of doing away with differing pension arrangements, 56 to be exact, for different categories of workers. This is a legacy of a long history of separate agreements on sector and category lines which have been a feature of the evolution of social welfare in Italy.
For over 15 years successive governments have not been able to come up with a positive answer to this union demand and have just let the pension system drift.

It was only under pressure from the 1992 currency crisis that the government of Prime Minister Giuliano Amato succeeded in getting parliament to approve a reorganisation of the pension system aimed essentially at achieving savings on spending.

This move, however, left unsolved the main problems of harmonising the different schemes as well as that of adapting the pension system to take account of the profound changes which had occurred in the labour market.

In 1994, faced with a new heavy cut in pensions spending and the laissez-faire type economic policies outlined by the government of Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi, the union movement decided to counter with a systematic reform proposal, combined with a tough line of resistance.

The proposal was aimed at getting to the heart of the crisis in the pension system and at the same time dealing with the linked issues of its economic sustainability and of its fairness and suitability in the context of changes in the labour market and in Italian society.

The defence of the public pay-as-you-go system was central to this approach which, after the defeat of the Berlusconi government, was taken on board in the pensions reform enacted by the government of Prime Minister Lamberto Dini.

This was the case not only because of the difficulty of earmarking extra resources in order to move towards privately funded schemes, given the state of the country's public finances. It also sprang from the conviction that public intervention could not be substituted on grounds of economic efficiency.
For objective reasons deriving from incomplete information the market cannot function properly. A system of privately funded pensions is not able to protect workers against the risk of inflation.
Private pension funds can play a top-up role but cannot replace a pay-as-you-go public pensions system.

In the face of the difficult problems deriving from demographic trends, the reform sought by the unions calls for a combination of measures based both on the pay-as-you-go principle and on a private funded system. This ensures a higher degree of public cover for workers with medium-to-low incomes and shifts a significant part of pensions cover for medium-to-high income and top-flight workers to the funds.

The Dini reform represents an important result, even if it cannot claim to have solved all the problems of fairness and financial and macroeconomic sustainability underlying the Italian social welfare system.

In fact the reform guarantees a dynamic eqilibrium in the long-term by linking pension benefits to an actuarial equivalent of the sum total of contributions paid over the whole of a working life and to the age at which a person retires, which a worker can choose between 57 and 65 years of age.

The method of calculating pensions which amounts to "a virtual funded system" (contributions paid in are are revalued at an interest rate equal to the growth rate of gross domestic product in an interest-bearing account from which benefits are subsequently drawn) is capable of ensuring the financial equilibrium of the pay-as-you-go system in response to demographic and economic changes.

The profoundly innovative scope of this reform which is recognised by the International Monetary Fund is in danger of being obscured by the debate in Italy over the excessive slowness of the reform and over the fact that older workers are left relatively unscathed.

It should be pointed out that the new contributory system already involves more than 70 percent of Italian workers. For the remaining 30 percent the reform provides for a gradual phasing out of seniority pensions -- pensions entitled to be drawn after paying contributions into the system for 35 years -- producing over a decade savings of the order of tens of trillions of lire.

The slow-acting nature of the reform is justified on grounds of maintaining social consensus. But also for economic reasons, more than political ones. As Nobel prize-winning economist Franco Modigliani has said one should never forget that in planning their spending people take into account their maturing pension rights.
Italy spends around two percent of GDP -- more than Germany and France -- on pensions, but overall about six percent less overall on social welfare spending.

Bringing pensions spending into line with the other main European countries has to be gradual and accompanied by the growth of pension funds. The pensions system must also be gradually freed from tasks which do not belong to it such as providing economic support for the employed and under-employed and aid for sectors such as commerce, artisans and farming.

At the same time as curtailing pensions spending, it is necessary to plan the growth of social spending in areas in which Italy is lagging behind the European Union. There is therefore no room for further cuts in social spending.

The debate has revived not because the Dini reform is not working but because after the discussions over the summer of our governors with other European partners it was decided to bring the ratio of net debt to gross domestic product to within three percent.
In order to attain this objective a very tough adjustment of state accounts was approved at the end of 1996 with the agreement of the unions.

Italy is running a record primary surplus (on its national account). The real issue remains therefore spending on interest (payments) and the solution to this problem lies above all in a fall in interest rates.
